People often say "brand" when they mean the logo. In strategy work we separate three ideas. Your **brand** is what people think and feel when they hear the business name: the memories, opinions and expectations stored in their heads. Your **brand identity** is the set of tools you control that trigger those memories: the name, logo, colours, packaging, photos and the way you write. Your **brand position** is the specific place you want to own in the customer's mind, compared with the other choices she has.

The word positioning was made popular by two American advertising men, **Al Ries and Jack Trout**, first in trade magazine articles and then in their 1981 book *Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind*. Their key point still holds: positioning is not what you do to a product, it is what you do to the mind of the buyer. You cannot add a position by printing a new flyer. You earn it by choosing a clear idea and repeating it, in words and in actions, until customers connect that idea with you.

A clear position is how one business stands out among many that sell almost the same thing.

A strong answer is narrow enough that some customers will say "this is not for me". That is a good sign. A position that tries to please everybody ends up meaning nothing to anybody.

Start with why, then be specific

Simon Sinek's well known TED talk describes the **Golden Circle**: why you do it, how you do it, and what you sell. Most businesses describe only the what ("we sell small chops"). Purpose gives a brand energy, but purpose alone is not positioning. "We want to make people happy" is a purpose many brands share. Positioning turns purpose into a specific, testable choice about a customer, an alternative and a difference.
Why unclear brands end up fighting on price

When customers see no real difference between sellers, the only thing left to compare is price. The seller then has to match every discount, and profit disappears quickly because discounts come straight out of profit, not out of costs.
Worked example: two small chops vendors, same cost
For example, Ada and Bisi both run small chops businesses in Port Harcourt. Each 100-piece office tray costs them about 60,000 naira (approximate) in ingredients, packaging, gas and transport.
Ada has no clear position. She sells at 75,000 naira. Profit per tray: 75,000 minus 60,000 = 15,000 naira.
A customer says another vendor is cheaper, so Ada gives 10% off: 10% of 75,000 = 7,500 naira. Her profit falls to 15,000 minus 7,500 = 7,500 naira. One discount halved her profit.

Bisi positions herself for office admins: hot delivery at the agreed time, a proper invoice and receipt, and a named contact who answers. She sells at 95,000 naira. Profit: 95,000 minus 60,000 = 35,000 naira.
Admins who have been embarrassed by late food before are happy to pay more for reliability, so Bisi rarely gets asked for a discount.
With the same costs, Bisi earns 35,000 naira per tray while Ada, after one discount, earns 7,500 naira. The difference is not the recipe, it is a clear, believable position for a specific buyer.
A position must be true

Never promise what the business cannot deliver every time. A broken promise damages the brand faster than having no promise. In Nigeria, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) protects consumers against misleading claims, and advertising is regulated by the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (ARCON). Build your position on things you can prove.
Common mistakes to avoid
Treating a new logo as a new strategy. Identity should express a position, not replace it.
Choosing a target of "everyone". Even large brands choose a core customer first.
Copying the leader's message. If the leader owns "cheapest", saying "cheapest" louder rarely works.
Forgetting that "do nothing" and "do it myself" are competitors too. A home cook is an alternative to a caterer.

Professional brand strategists use a small, precise vocabulary. Learn these terms well, because clients, agencies and marketing teams use them in briefs and meetings, and because each term forces a decision.
Term
Plain meaning
Target segment
The specific group of customers you are built for, described by needs and situation, not only age and location
The category or set of alternatives the customer compares you with
Points of parity
The basics you must match so you are not rejected (for example, clean kitchen, fair price range)
Points of difference
The few things you do better or differently that the target truly values
Reason to believe
The proof that makes your difference credible

The full bundle of benefits a customer gets for the price she pays

Positioning starts by choosing a specific target segment, not 'everyone'.
Parity first, then difference

Kevin Lane Keller, Brian Sternthal and Alice Tybout explained in a 2002 Harvard Business Review article that strong positioning needs both **points of parity** and **points of difference** within a clear **frame of reference**. Parity gets you onto the shortlist. Difference wins the choice. A hair salon that offers a unique style but keeps customers waiting three hours has a difference but fails on parity, so customers leave anyway.

A good point of difference passes three tests. It is **relevant**: the target segment actually cares. It is **distinctive**: competitors do not already own it. It is **deliverable**: the business can keep it true every week, not just during a launch. If a difference fails any one test, drop it or fix the operation behind it first.
The positioning statement

A positioning statement is an internal sentence, not an advert. It guides decisions about products, prices, photos and posts. A widely used template, popularised by Geoffrey Moore in the technology world, is:
Parts of a positioning statement
For (target segment)
Who (need or problem)
Our brand is (category)
That (key benefit)
Unlike (main alternative)
Because (reason to believe)
Read left to right: each part narrows the idea until it can guide real decisions.
Worked example: positioning a tutoring centre in Abuja
For example, Hauwa runs a small after-school tutoring centre in Gwarinpa, Abuja. Her first draft said: 'We offer quality education for all children.'
Target: she checks her records. Most paying parents have children in JSS3 or SS3 preparing for BECE, WAEC or NECO, and both parents work full time.
Need: these parents worry about exam results but cannot supervise homework on weekdays.
Frame of reference: home lesson teachers and larger tutorial centres.
Points of parity: qualified tutors, safe premises, fees in the normal range for the area.
Point of difference she can deliver: a short WhatsApp progress report to each parent every Friday, with the topics covered and one score.
Reason to believe: sample reports (with names hidden) and her published weekly schedule.

Her statement: 'For working parents in Gwarinpa whose children are preparing for BECE or WAEC, Hauwa's Study Hub is an exam-focused tutoring centre that keeps you informed every week. Unlike home lesson teachers, we send a written progress report every Friday, so you always know where your child stands.'

Before you keep any statement, run the **swap test**. Replace your brand name with a competitor's name and read the statement again. If it still sounds true for the competitor, your point of difference is not really different, and customers will not be able to tell you apart either. Hauwa's statement passes, because no nearby centre sends a weekly written report. A statement like 'quality tutoring with caring teachers' fails, because every centre in Abuja could say it.
Write three, keep one
Draft three different statements built on three different points of difference, then test them with real customers (you will learn how in Module 2). The first idea is rarely the strongest.
Brand personality

Personality describes how the brand behaves and sounds, as if it were a person. Researcher Jennifer Aaker identified five broad dimensions of brand personality: **sincerity** (honest, warm), **excitement** (daring, lively), **competence** (reliable, intelligent), **sophistication** (refined, upper class) and **ruggedness** (tough, outdoorsy). Most brands lead with one or two. Hauwa's centre should lead with competence and sincerity. A party DJ brand would lead with excitement.
Pick one or two dimensions, not all five.
Turn each into behaviour: for competence, 'we reply within two hours and never miss a report'.
Check that the personality fits the target: busy parents want calm and reliable, not loud and trendy.
Statement versus tagline

The positioning statement is long and internal. A tagline is a short public line that may come from it later. Hauwa's tagline might become 'Know where your child stands, every Friday.' Never publish the raw statement as your slogan.
Parity gets you considered; difference gets you chosen.
A point of difference must be relevant, distinctive and deliverable.
The positioning statement names target, need, category, benefit, alternative and proof.
Personality is shown through behaviour, not adjectives alone.

Positioning only works once you know whose mind you are trying to win. Marketers call the full process **segmentation, targeting and positioning (STP)**: split the market into groups with different needs, choose the group you will serve best, then position for that group. Lesson 2 gave you the positioning tools. This lesson is about the choice that comes before them.
Groups of people sorted into different coloured clusters
Segmentation splits one market into groups with different needs, so you can choose where to compete.
Four ways to split a market
Basis
What you look at
Example for a shea butter brand
Needs
The problem or job the buyer is solving
Dry skin relief, baby skin care, hair growth routine
Occasion
When and why the purchase happens
Daily use, gifts, wedding favours, travel
Price tier
How much the buyer expects to pay and why
Open market loose butter, mid-range branded tubs, premium gift jars
Channel
Where she prefers to buy
Open market, pharmacy shelf, WhatsApp vendor, Jumia, diaspora order

Age, gender and location (demographics) still matter, but needs and occasions usually explain buying better. Two 30-year-old women in Kano may buy the same product for completely different reasons, one for her own skin and one as a wedding gift. Each reason needs a different message and package.
What makes a segment worth choosing
Five tests of a useful segment
Measurable: you can estimate size
Substantial: big enough to pay
Reachable: you can get to them
Different: they respond differently
Actionable: you can serve them
If a segment fails any test, it is an idea, not a target.

These five tests are a long-standing checklist in marketing textbooks. In African markets, **reachable** deserves extra attention. Can you reach the segment through channels you can afford: WhatsApp groups, church or mosque networks, market associations, Instagram, local radio, or a pharmacy owner who trusts you? A segment you cannot reach cheaply is not your segment yet.
Score your options with numbers
Worked example: choosing a target for a shea butter brand

For example, Zainab processes clean, filtered shea butter near Tamale and sells it across Ghana and to Nigerian buyers online. She compares three segments using four criteria, each scored 1 (poor) to 5 (strong), with weights she agrees with her sister.
Weights: size 30%, willingness to pay 30%, reachability 25%, fit with her strengths 15%.
Segment A, mothers buying for babies: size 4, pay 3, reach 4, fit 5. Score = 4x0.30 + 3x0.30 + 4x0.25 + 5x0.15 = 1.20 + 0.90 + 1.00 + 0.75 = 3.85.
Segment B, wedding favour planners: size 2, pay 5, reach 3, fit 3. Score = 0.60 + 1.50 + 0.75 + 0.45 = 3.30.
Segment C, diaspora natural hair buyers: size 3, pay 5, reach 2, fit 4. Score = 0.90 + 1.50 + 0.50 + 0.60 = 3.50.
She checks that her weights add up: 30 + 30 + 25 + 15 = 100%.

Segment A wins with 3.85, so Zainab positions first for mothers who want a gentle, clean product for babies. She keeps Segment C as a second target for later, once she has a reliable shipping partner.
Health claims need care

When a segment is about babies, skin or health, never claim the product treats or cures a condition unless you have proper approval. In Nigeria, cosmetics and similar products must meet NAFDAC requirements, and claims on labels and adverts must be honest. Position on things like clean processing and gentle use, which you can show, rather than medical benefits.
African market realities that change targeting
**Informal and formal side by side.** The same customer may buy loose products in the open market and branded ones online. Decide which buying moment you are targeting.
**Trust travels through people.** Referrals in WhatsApp groups, religious communities and associations often matter more than adverts. Target segments where you already have trusted links.
**Price sensitivity is real but not universal.** Many buyers trade down when prices rise, but some segments, such as gift buyers or busy professionals, still pay for convenience and reliability.
**Diaspora buyers** in the UK, US and elsewhere often want home products they trust, but shipping, customs rules and payment options must be solved before you target them.
**Mobile first.** Most of your target will see your brand on a phone screen first, so your position must be clear in a WhatsApp profile or an Instagram bio of a few lines.

A strong brand often starts narrow and widens later. Owning one segment well gives you referrals, testimonials and cash, which pay for the next segment. Trying to serve five segments at once usually means five half-finished messages and confused customers.

Check your choice with the people who will carry it out. If the owner, staff or rider dislike serving the chosen segment, the position will slowly fade in daily practice. Zainab's team, for example, enjoys explaining gentle use to new mothers, which makes the baby care segment easier to keep.
One primary, one secondary
Write down one primary segment that gets most of your effort and money, and at most one secondary segment. Everything else goes on a 'later' list.

Brand strategy is built on evidence, not on the owner's opinion. The good news is that the core tools are free and work on a smartphone: WhatsApp, Google Forms, Google Sheets, Google Maps reviews, Instagram and a notebook. What makes them professional is how you use them.
A person reviewing charts and marketing data on a screen
Research turns guesses about customers and competitors into evidence you can show a client.
Tool 1: the customer interview

Talk to real buyers, one at a time, by phone, video call or in person. A practical starting point is five to eight people from your primary segment. Stop when you keep hearing the same answers. Ask about **past behaviour**, not opinions about the future, because people are poor at predicting what they will do.
"Tell me about the last time you bought [product]. What was happening that day?"
"What else did you consider, including doing it yourself or not buying?"
"What almost stopped you from buying?"
"How would you describe this business to a friend?"
"What would make you stop using it?"

These questions follow the **jobs to be done** idea described by Clayton Christensen and colleagues in Harvard Business Review: customers "hire" a product to make progress in a particular situation. A working mother does not just buy laundry service. She hires it to get her Saturday back and to look neat at work on Monday. That job, not the product feature, is what your position must speak to.

Take notes in the customer's own words, not your summary of them. After each interview, write the three most important things you heard within the hour, while you still remember the tone. Never argue or explain your product during an interview; you are there to learn, not to sell. If someone criticises the business, thank them, because complaints often point straight to a point of parity that needs fixing.
Tool 2: review and comment mining

Open Google Maps reviews, Instagram comments, Facebook pages and Jumia or Konga reviews for your business and three competitors. Copy phrases customers repeat into a sheet with three columns: praise, complaint, exact words. Customers' own words often make the best taglines and captions later, because they sound natural to other customers.
Tool 3: the competitor audit grid

For each competitor record the same six things: who they seem to target, their main promise, price range, channels, tone of voice, and the proof they show. Look at their WhatsApp business profile, Instagram bio, signage and how they reply to a test enquiry. Keep the grid factual; you are mapping positions, not judging people.

Finally, make a test enquiry yourself, as a normal customer would. Note how fast each competitor replies, what they ask, and how they describe themselves. These small moments often reveal a competitor's real position better than their adverts do.
Tool 4: the perceptual map

A perceptual map places brands on two axes that customers actually care about, so you can see crowded areas and empty spaces. Choose the axes from your interviews and reviews, not from your own guesses. Price and quality are common, but speed, convenience, style or trust may matter more in your category.
Perceptual map: laundry services in Ibadan
Fast but expensive
Fast and affordable (gap)
Slow and expensive
Slow but cheap
Most competitors cluster in two boxes; the empty box is a possible position if the business can deliver it.
Price: high to low
Turnaround: fast to slow
Worked example: finding a gap in the laundry market
For example, Tolu runs a two-person laundry in Bodija, Ibadan, and wants a sharper position. She audits four competitors and interviews six customers.
Audit: two hotel-linked dry cleaners charge about 1,500 naira (approximate) per shirt and return in 24 hours. Two neighbourhood washers charge about 400 naira per shirt but take five to seven days.
Interviews: five of six customers mention ironed work shirts ready for Monday as the real need. Four mention fear of lost items.
Reviews: competitors' complaints repeat the words 'lost my shirt' and 'they kept shifting the date'.
Map: nobody occupies 'affordable and fast'. Tolu checks her capacity: with pickup on Friday evening and return on Sunday evening she can handle about 40 shirts a week.
She prices at 700 naira per shirt with a tagged-item list sent on WhatsApp at pickup.

Tolu's position: weekend work-shirt service for young professionals, back by Sunday night, every item listed and tagged. It comes straight from customer words and an empty space on the map, and it is something she can deliver.
Respect customers' data

Ask permission before recording a call, tell people how you will use their answers, and do not share names, phone numbers or screenshots outside the project. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for handling personal data, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission. When in doubt, store answers without names (Customer 1, Customer 2) and delete raw recordings after the project.
Use a free survey for numbers
Interviews give you depth. A short Google Form sent to a WhatsApp customer list can then check how common an answer is. Keep it under eight questions so people finish it on a phone.
Interview about past behaviour, not future opinions.

Clients do not pay for frameworks. They pay for a clear decision they can act on. A good workflow gets you from a messy first conversation to that decision on time, with the client involved at the right moments so there are no surprises at the end.
A person moving through connected steps of a process
A visible process keeps the client involved and the project on schedule.
A four-week positioning project
Week 1: brief and discovery
Week 2: customer and competitor research
Week 3: insights and positioning routes
Week 4: testing, decision, handover
Each week ends with something the client can see, so feedback comes early, not at the end.
Stage by stage

**Brief and kickoff.** Agree the business goal (for example, raise average order value or win office clients), the decision-maker, the budget, and what is out of scope. Write it in a one-page brief and get a 'yes' in writing.
**Discovery.** Interview the owner and one or two staff. Ask what the business does best, what customers praise, what they would never do, and where money is lost.
**Research.** Use the tools from Lesson 1: customer interviews, review mining, competitor grid, perceptual map.
**Synthesis.** Group findings and write insights. An insight has two parts: what you observed, and why it matters for the brand.
**Positioning routes.** Write two or three distinct routes. Each route has a target, a point of difference, a reason to believe and a sample tagline or WhatsApp bio.
**Testing and decision.** Show the routes to customers, count reactions, and recommend one route to the client with your reasons.
**Handover.** Deliver the strategy document and a short session showing staff how to use it.
Writing insights, not just findings

A finding is a fact: "Four of six customers mentioned lost items." An insight explains what it means: "Customers fear losing clothes more than they care about price, so visible tracking could be our strongest proof." Aim for five to seven insights. Each positioning route should be built on at least one of them.
Testing routes with real customers

Put each route on a simple card or WhatsApp image with the same layout so only the idea changes. Show the cards in a different order to each person, so the first card does not always win. Ask three questions: which one is most appealing to you, which one would you trust, and which one, if any, would make you willing to pay a little more.
Worked example: reading test results
For example, Ifeoma is positioning a home cleaning service in Lekki. She tests three routes with 12 customers from her target segment of busy two-income households.
Route A, 'Vetted, trained cleaners you can trust with your keys': chosen as most appealing by 7 of 12 people. 7 divided by 12 = 0.583, about 58%.
Route B, 'Spotless in three hours or we come back free': 3 of 12, which is 25%.
Route C, 'Eco-friendly cleaning products': 2 of 12, about 17%. Check: 7 + 3 + 2 = 12.
On 'which would you trust', Route A wins again with 8 of 12, about 67%.
Several people who chose Route B said they had been let down by guarantees before.

Ifeoma recommends Route A. She also notes that 12 people is a small sample, so the result guides the decision but does not prove it. She plans to track enquiries for three months after launch to confirm the route works.

Also listen to the reasons people give, not only their choice. A route that wins appeal but loses on trust may need stronger proof before launch. A route that nobody picks first but several people call 'believable' might become a supporting pillar later rather than the main promise.
Small samples, honest language
With 10 to 20 people you can see strong preferences, but do not present percentages as if they describe the whole market. Say '7 of the 12 customers we spoke to', not '58% of Lagos'.

A positioning strategy only creates value when everyone uses it: the owner, staff, the designer, the person replying on WhatsApp. The brand guideline translates strategy into rules people can follow on a busy day. For a small business it can be five to eight pages, not a hundred.
A person checking a set of approved documents
A short, clear guideline turns strategy into rules the whole team can follow.
The messaging house

A messaging house is a simple structure used by many brand teams. The **roof** is the brand promise in one line. Under it stand **three pillars**, the main messages that support the promise. The **foundation** is the proof for each pillar: facts, processes, testimonials, numbers the business can show.
Worked example: a messaging house for Tolu's laundry
For example, Tolu from Lesson 1 has chosen the position 'weekend work-shirt service for young professionals, back by Sunday night, every item listed and tagged'.
Roof (promise): 'Your work week starts neat. Every shirt back by Sunday night.'
Pillar 1, On time: Friday pickup, Sunday return. Proof: delivery log showing return times.
Pillar 2, Nothing lost: every item tagged and listed on WhatsApp at pickup. Proof: sample item list and tag photo.
Pillar 3, Work-ready finish: shirts pressed and hung, not folded. Proof: before and after photos with customer permission.
Elevator pitch: 'We collect your work shirts on Friday, tag and list every item, and return them pressed by Sunday night, so Monday morning is easy.'
Every caption, flyer, reply and price list now has a clear source. If a message does not support one of the three pillars, Tolu does not post it.

Clients usually arrive with a solution already in mind: "we need a new logo", "we need a rebrand", "we need to go viral". Discovery is your chance to understand the business before agreeing with them. Good discovery protects the client's money and your reputation, because the right diagnosis makes the work succeed.
Two people in a structured conversation across a table
Discovery is a structured conversation that finds the real problem before any proposal is written.
Before the call

Send a short Google Form or WhatsApp list of questions a day before. It saves call time and shows how organised the client is. Six questions are enough: what the business sells, who buys most, what has changed recently, what result they want in six months, who makes the final decision, and the budget range they have in mind.
A 45-minute discovery call
Minutes 0 to 5: thank them, confirm the time, explain the purpose: to understand, not to sell.
Minutes 5 to 25: business and customers. Use the question bank below and take notes.
Minutes 25 to 35: competitors and what makes them different, in their own words.
Minutes 35 to 40: success. 'If this works, what will be different in six months?'
Minutes 40 to 45: next steps. Tell them when your proposal or recommendation will arrive.

Listening matters more than asking. Let short silences sit, because owners often add the most useful detail after a pause. Write down their exact words, especially how they describe customers and competitors. At the end of each section, summarise back in one sentence, for example 'So your best customers are office admins who reorder when delivery is on time, is that right?' The client either confirms or corrects you, and both help.
The five whys
When a client names a symptom, ask "why" several times, gently, until you reach a cause you can act on. Five is a guide, not a rule; stop when the answer points to something specific.
Worked example: the cake shop that wanted a rebrand
For example, Chioma owns a cake shop in Enugu. She says sales of celebration cakes fell over six months and asks for a new logo and name.
Why did sales fall? 'Fewer repeat orders from people who bought before.'
Why fewer repeat orders? 'Some customers complained.'
Why did they complain? Chioma checks her WhatsApp: 9 of the last 30 cake orders had complaints, and 7 of those 9 were about cakes arriving damaged.
Why were cakes damaged? 'We switched to cheaper, thinner boxes and a new dispatch rider.'
Why the switch? 'To save about 500 naira (approximate) per order.'

The root cause is delivery packaging, not the logo. 9 of 30 is 30% of orders with complaints, and 7 of 9, about 78% of complaints, are about damage. The honest recommendation: fix boxes and delivery first, then position the shop on 'arrives perfect' with a photo sent before dispatch. A new logo now would have cost money and changed nothing.

When the problem is not branding

Positioning cannot fix a poor product, a broken delivery process, prices far above what customers will pay, or a cash flow crisis. If discovery shows one of these, say it clearly and in writing. You can still offer help: a smaller project, a referral to someone better placed, or a positioning project once the operation is fixed. Clients remember honest advice and often come back.
Red flags to notice
No clear decision-maker, or a decision-maker who will not attend any meeting.
A deadline that leaves no time for research, for example 'launch on Friday'.
Expecting guaranteed sales numbers or 'going viral'.
Refusing to share basic facts such as price lists or customer feedback.
Pressure to start work before any deposit or written agreement.
Protect yourself and the client

Never ask clients for passwords, bank PINs or OTPs. If you need access to a social account, ask them to add you as a team member through the platform's settings. Keep client information confidential and store it only in the project folder.

From hours to a fee
Worked example: pricing the three packages
For example, Amaka is a marketing professional in Lagos building a brand strategy practice on the side. Her figures are illustrative and her prices approximate.
Income goal: 600,000 naira a month from this work. Billable hours she can realistically sell: 60 a month.
Minimum hourly rate: 600,000 divided by 60 = 10,000 naira per hour.
Full Project: 30 hours x 10,000 = 300,000 naira. She adds 15% for meetings and revisions: 300,000 x 1.15 = 345,000. She rounds to 350,000 naira.
Sprint: 12 hours x 10,000 = 120,000. Plus 15% = 138,000. Rounded: 140,000 naira.
Retainer: 8 hours x 10,000 = 80,000 naira a month.
Value check for a client like Bisi from Module 1: if a clearer position adds 20,000 naira profit per tray on 4 trays a month, that is 80,000 naira a month, or 960,000 naira a year.
Amaka's fees cover her time, and the Full Project at 350,000 naira is well below the yearly value it could create for a client like Bisi. She explains the price using the value, not her hours.
Your rate is a floor, not the price

The hourly calculation tells you the lowest fee that keeps you in business. The final price also depends on the client's size and the value the work can create. A small trader and a mid-sized manufacturer should not pay the same for the same hours.

Keep a simple record of actual hours for every project, broken down by stage. After three projects, compare actual hours with your estimates. If research always takes 14 hours instead of 10, update your package hours and fees, rather than quietly working unpaid hours on every job.

From enquiry to kickoff
Enquiry
Discovery call
Proposal within 3 days
Signed agreement and deposit
Kickoff meeting
Work starts only after the agreement and deposit, never before.
**Our understanding**: the client's situation and goal in their own words from discovery.
**Approach**: the stages from Module 2, in plain language.
**Deliverables**: exactly what they receive, for example 'one positioning statement, one messaging house, a 6-page guideline'.
**Timeline**: dates for each check-in and the final handover.
**Investment**: the package price and what it includes. Offering two options (Sprint and Full Project) lets the client choose instead of saying no.
**Terms**: 50% deposit to start, 50% on delivery, payment by bank transfer or a Paystack payment link, and how long the offer is valid.
**Next step**: one clear action, such as 'reply YES and I will send the invoice'.
Presenting the price

Send the proposal, then offer a 20-minute call to walk through it, so the client hears your reasoning instead of jumping straight to the number. If they say it is too expensive, do not cut the price of the same work. Offer a smaller scope instead: the Sprint instead of the Full Project, fewer interviews, or the guideline later. Cutting price without cutting scope teaches the client that your first figure was not real. A retainer works best after a project, when the client has seen the value and wants help keeping the brand consistent month by month.
Scope control

Most project problems come from vague scope. Write limits into the proposal: the number of customer interviews (for example, eight), the number of positioning routes (three), revision rounds on the final document (two), and what is **not** included, such as logo design, website building, paid adverts or printing. When the client asks for more, send a short written change request with the extra hours, the fee and the new deadline, and wait for a 'yes' before doing it.
Payment safety

Confirm every payment in your own bank or Paystack app before starting work. Screenshots of transfers can be faked. Never share OTPs or PINs, and be wary of 'clients' who overpay and ask for a refund of the difference, a common scam pattern.

Clients buy strategy from people they trust. Trust comes from showing your thinking, leading a room well and reporting results honestly. This lesson turns your course project into proof and gives you a plan to find paying work.

A small portfolio of honest case studies is the strongest sales tool for strategy work.
The case study
**Client and challenge**: who they are and what was wrong, in two or three sentences.
**What you did**: the research, insights and routes, with one image such as the perceptual map.
**The position**: the final statement and the messaging house.
**What changed**: only measured results, with dates, for example enquiries before and after.
**Client quote**: only with written permission, word for word.
Honesty rules for portfolios

Label practice projects as practice. Do not claim results you did not measure or that other factors caused. Hide customer names and numbers unless the client agrees in writing. One honest case study is worth more than five inflated ones.
Leading a positioning workshop

A workshop helps a team agree on the position together, so they own it. Keep it to two hours, with the owner and two to five key staff. You need sticky notes or a WhatsApp poll, markers, and your research summary.

As facilitator you stay neutral, keep time, make sure quieter staff speak, and bring the conversation back to customer evidence when people argue from personal taste. Front-line staff such as riders and sales attendants often know customers best; invite them.

Dot voting is simple: each person gets three sticky dots, or three votes in a WhatsApp poll, and places them on the differences they believe customers value most. It gives quieter people an equal voice. End the workshop by reading the agreed actions aloud and sending them in writing the same day.
The handover presentation

When the project ends, present the strategy in about 45 minutes: the goal you agreed, what customers told you, the routes you tested and the results, the final position, and exactly how to use the guideline from tomorrow. Leave time for questions from staff. A week after handover, ask the client for a short written testimonial while the work is fresh, and ask permission to use it.

Agree a few measures before launch so you can compare. Useful ones for small businesses: enquiries per week, the share of enquiries that mention the promise, conversion rate (orders divided by enquiries), average order value, number of discount requests, and repeat customers.
Worked example: three months after launch
For example, Tolu's laundry relaunched with its weekend work-shirt position. She logs WhatsApp enquiries and orders in a simple Google Sheet.
Month before launch: 40 enquiries, 10 orders. Conversion = 10 divided by 40 = 25%.
Third month after launch: 45 enquiries, 15 orders. Conversion = 15 divided by 45 = 33%.
Average order before: 3,500 naira (5 shirts x 700). After: 4,900 naira (7 shirts x 700), because customers send all their work shirts at once.
Discount requests fell from 6 to 2 a month.
She notes other changes in the same period, such as a new estate opening nearby, so she does not credit everything to the brand.
Conversion rose from 25% to about 33% and average order value from 3,500 to 4,900 naira. The evidence supports the position, and Tolu has an honest result for a case study.

Module 1 video
Brand, position and target: choose where you will win
Brand, position and target: choose where you will win.
This is the video for module one of Brand Strategy and Positioning.
Three ideas
A brand is not the logo
Brand: what people think and feel
Identity: the tools you control
Position: the place you choose to own
People often say brand when they mean the logo. Your brand is what people think and feel when they hear the business name.
Your brand identity is the set of tools you control: the name, logo, colours, packaging, photos and the way you write.

Your position is the specific place you want to own in the customer's mind, compared with her other choices. You cannot print a position on a flyer. You earn it by repeating one clear idea, in words and actions.
Every brand strategy
Five decisions to write down
Target: who exactly are we for?
Frame of reference: compared with what?
Difference: why choose us?
Proof: why believe it?
Personality: how do we sound?
A brand strategy answers five questions. First, the target. Not everybody who eats, but, for example, office admins in Port Harcourt who order snacks for meetings.
Second, what will she compare us with? Third, why choose us? Quality and good service is what every competitor says. Delivered hot, on the agreed time, with a proper invoice, is a real difference.
Fourth, the proof, like an on-time delivery log. Fifth, the personality: calm, punctual, polite.
A strong answer is narrow enough that some customers say, this is not for me. That is a good sign.
Worked example
Same cost, very different profit
For example, Ada and Bisi both sell small chops trays in Port Harcourt. Each tray costs about 60,000 naira.
Ada's price, no clear position
Ada's profit after 10% off
Bisi's price, positioned
Bisi's profit per tray
Naira figures are approximate.
When customers see no real difference, the only thing left to compare is price.

Ada has no clear position. She sells at 75,000 naira, a profit of 15,000. A customer says another vendor is cheaper, so she gives 10 percent off, 7,500 naira. Her profit falls to 7,500. One discount halved it, because discounts come straight out of profit.

Bisi positions herself for office admins: hot delivery at the agreed time, a proper invoice, and a contact who answers. She sells at 95,000 and earns 35,000 per tray. Admins rarely ask her for a discount.
Point of difference
Three tests for your difference
The target segment actually cares about it.
Competitors do not already own it.
You can keep it true every week, not just at launch.

First, match the basics, the points of parity, so you are not rejected. Parity gets you on the shortlist. Difference wins the choice. A good point of difference is relevant: the target actually cares.
It is distinctive: competitors do not already own it.
And it is deliverable, every week. A broken promise damages the brand faster than having no promise. Build your position only on things you can prove.
Hauwa writes a positioning statement
Swap test: put a competitor's name in. Still true? Not different.
For: working parents in Gwarinpa
Who: have children facing BECE or WAEC
Is: an exam-focused tutoring centre
Unlike: home lesson teachers
Because: a progress report every Friday
A positioning statement is an internal sentence, not an advert. For example, Hauwa runs a tutoring centre in Abuja. Her first draft said: we offer quality education for all children.

Her records show most paying parents both work full time, with children preparing for BECE or WAEC. So: for working parents in Gwarinpa whose children face these exams, Hauwa's Study Hub is an exam-focused tutoring centre.
Unlike home lesson teachers, she sends a written progress report every Friday, so parents always know where their child stands.
Now run the swap test. Put a competitor's name in. Quality tutoring with caring teachers fails, because every centre could say it. Hauwa's passes.
Targeting
Zainab scores three segments
Weights must add up to 100%. Choose one primary segment.
Weights: size 30, pay 30, reach 25, fit 15
A: mothers buying for babies = 3.85
B: wedding favour planners = 3.30
C: diaspora hair buyers = 3.50
Primary A; C kept for later

Positioning only works once you know whose mind you are winning. For example, Zainab sells shea butter from near Tamale. She scores three segments from 1 to 5 on size, willingness to pay, reachability, and fit, with weights that add up to 100 percent.
Mothers buying for babies score 3.85. Wedding favour planners score 3.30. Diaspora natural hair buyers score 3.50.
So she positions first for mothers, and keeps diaspora buyers for later, once she has a reliable shipping partner.
Because this segment is about babies and skin, she never claims the product treats or cures anything. She positions on clean processing and gentle use, which she can show.
Before you choose
Check your segment against five tests. Measurable, substantial, reachable, different and actionable. If it fails one, it is an idea, not a target.
Reachable matters most here. Can you reach them cheaply, through WhatsApp groups, church or mosque networks, or market associations?
Key points
Remember
Brand lives in the customer's mind
Decide target, frame, difference, proof
No difference means price fights
Relevant, distinctive, deliverable
Segment, target, then position
To remember. Your brand lives in the customer's mind. Decide your target, frame, difference, proof and personality. Without a difference, customers compare price only.
Make your difference relevant, distinctive and deliverable. And segment, target, then position.

Research, test and write it down: evidence-based positioning
Research, test and write it down: evidence-based positioning.
This is the video for module two of Brand Strategy and Positioning.
Why this matters
Evidence, not the owner's opinion
Customer interviews
Review and comment mining
Competitor audit grid
Perceptual map
Brand strategy is built on evidence, not the owner's opinion. Interview real buyers, and mine reviews and comments for the exact words customers repeat.
Then audit competitors on the same six points, and draw a perceptual map: two axes customers care about, to show crowded spaces and empty ones.
Ask about the past, not the future
Tell me about the last time you bought
What else did you consider?
What almost stopped you from buying?
How would you describe it to a friend?
What would make you stop using it?

Talk to five to eight people from your primary segment. Ask about past behaviour, because people are poor at predicting what they will do. Tell me about the last time you bought. What else did you consider?
What almost stopped you? How would you describe it to a friend? What would make you stop?
Customers hire a product to do a job. A working mother hires a laundry to get her Saturday back. Write their own words, and never sell during an interview.
Worked example
Tolu finds a gap in the laundry market
For example, Tolu runs a two-person laundry in Bodija, Ibadan. She audits four competitors.
Dry cleaners, 24 hours
Neighbourhood, 5 to 7 days
Tolu: back by Sunday
Per shirt. Naira prices are approximate.
Two dry cleaners charge about 1,500 naira per shirt and return in 24 hours. Two neighbourhood washers charge about 400 but take five to seven days. Nobody is both affordable and fast.
In interviews, five of six customers want ironed work shirts ready for Monday, and reviews repeat 'lost my shirt'. She checks she can handle about 40 shirts a week, and prices at 700 naira.
Her position: a weekend work-shirt service, back by Sunday night, every item listed and tagged.
Safety first
Ask before recording a call, and tell people how you will use their answers.
Never share names, numbers or screenshots outside the project.
Use Customer 1, Customer 2. Delete raw recordings after the project.
Research means handling personal data. Ask permission before recording a call, and tell people how you will use their answers.
Do not share names, phone numbers or screenshots outside the project. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for handling personal data.
When in doubt, store answers as Customer 1 and Customer 2, and delete raw recordings afterwards.
Workflow
An insight says what you saw, and why it matters for the brand.
Week 1: signed brief and discovery
Clients pay for a clear decision. In week 1, agree the goal, the decision-maker and the scope in a one-page brief, and get a yes in writing. In week 2, do the research.

In week 3, turn findings into insights. Four of six customers mentioned lost items is a finding. Customers fear losing clothes more than price, so tracking could be our proof, is an insight. Build two or three routes on them.
In week 4, test the routes, recommend one, and hand over.
Ifeoma tests three routes
Say '7 of the 12 customers we spoke to', not '58% of Lagos'.
Same card layout, shuffled order
A, vetted cleaners: 7 of 12, about 58%
B, spotless or free: 3 of 12, 25%
C, eco-friendly: 2 of 12, about 17%
Trust: A wins again, 8 of 12
For example, Ifeoma is positioning a home cleaning service in Lekki. She puts each route on a card with the same layout, and shows them in a different order to each of 12 customers.
Route A, vetted, trained cleaners you can trust with your keys, is chosen by 7 of 12. Route B gets 3, and Route C gets 2.
On trust, Route A wins again, 8 of 12. She recommends it. But 12 people is a small sample, so she reports it honestly and tracks enquiries for three months after launch.
Brand guidelines
Tolu's messaging house
Roof: every shirt back by Sunday night
Pillar: on time, with a delivery log
Pillar: nothing lost, every item tagged
Pillar: work-ready, pressed and hung
A guideline turns strategy into rules people can follow on a busy day. Start with a messaging house. The roof is the promise: your work week starts neat, every shirt back by Sunday night.
Three pillars hold it up, each with proof: on time, shown by a delivery log. Nothing lost, shown by the tagged item list. And work-ready, shown by before and after photos.
If a post does not support a pillar, Tolu does not post it.
We are, we are not
Tone rules work best as pairs. Tolu's brand is calm, short and clear, warm, and honest about delays.
It is not loud, not full of slang, not stiff, and never makes excuses.
Quality check
The consistency audit
Fix easy, high-visibility items first: bios and greetings.
List every place customers meet you
Check: promise, tone, current details
Score: 6 of 10 pass = 60%
Fix bios and greetings first
Before handover, list every touchpoint. Check each one for the promise, the tone, and current prices and contacts.
If 6 of 10 pass, consistency is 60 percent. Fix the easy, visible items first.
Key points
Remember
Interview about past behaviour
Ask permission; store without names
Insights say why a finding matters
Test routes fairly, report honestly
Promise, three pillars, real proof

To remember. Interview about past behaviour. Ask permission and store data without names. Turn findings into insights. Test routes fairly and report small samples honestly. And build one promise on three pillars with real proof.

Discovery, proposals and proof: run positioning as a practice
Discovery, proposals and proof: run positioning as a practice.
This is the video for module three of Brand Strategy and Positioning.
Why this matters
Clients arrive with a solution in mind
Discovery finds the real problem
Clear packages make work easy to buy
Scope limits protect your time
Honest results build trust

Clients usually arrive saying, we need a new logo, or we need to go viral. Discovery is your chance to understand the business before agreeing. The right diagnosis protects the client's money and your reputation.
Then clear packages, clear limits, and honest results turn your skill into a practice clients trust.
A 45-minute discovery agenda
0 to 5: purpose is to understand, not sell
5 to 25: business and customers
25 to 35: competitors, in their words
35 to 40: what success looks like
40 to 45: next steps and dates
Send a six-question form a day before. On the call, start by explaining the purpose: to understand, not to sell.

Spend most of the time on the business and its customers, then competitors. Who are your best customers? When you lose a sale, who wins it? Let short silences sit, because owners often add the most useful detail after a pause.
Ask: if this works, what will be different in six months? Then tell them when your proposal will arrive.
Five whys
The cake shop that wanted a rebrand
If the problem is not branding, say so clearly and in writing.
Why did sales fall? Fewer repeat orders
Why? Customers complained
Why? 7 of 9 complaints: damaged cakes
Why? Thinner boxes, a new rider
Why? To save about 500 naira an order
For example, Chioma owns a cake shop in Enugu. Sales fell for six months, and she asks for a new logo and name. Ask why, gently. Fewer repeat orders. Why? Customers complained.
She checks WhatsApp: 9 of the last 30 orders had complaints, and 7 of those 9 were cakes arriving damaged.
Why? She switched to cheaper, thinner boxes and a new rider, to save about 500 naira an order.
The root cause is packaging, not the logo. A new logo would have cost money and changed nothing. So fix delivery first, then position on arrives perfect.
Worked example
Pricing three packages
For example, Amaka in Lagos wants 600,000 naira a month and can sell 60 hours.
Minimum rate, per hour
Sprint: 12 hours + 15%
Full Project: 30 hours + 15%
Retainer: 8 hours a month
Illustrative, approximate naira figures.
Strategy is thinking work, so clients cannot see it like a cake or a dress. Clear packages make it easy to buy. Amaka divides 600,000 naira by 60 hours: her minimum rate is 10,000 naira an hour.
A Sprint is about 12 hours. She adds 15 percent for meetings and revisions, and rounds to 140,000. A Full Project of 30 hours becomes 350,000.
A monthly retainer of 8 hours is 80,000 naira.
Her rate is a floor, not the price. If a clearer position could add 960,000 naira a year for a client like Bisi, 350,000 is easy to explain. She explains price with value, not hours.
Proposals
Protect the project and yourself
Say how many interviews, routes and revisions, and what is not included, like logos.
Extra asks get a written note with hours, fee and new date. Wait for a yes.
50% deposit first. Confirm it in your own app. Never ask for or share passwords, PINs or OTPs.
Most project problems come from vague scope. Write limits into the proposal: for example eight interviews, three routes, two revision rounds, and no logo design or adverts.

When the client asks for more, send a short written change request with the extra hours, fee and new deadline. If they say the price is too high, offer a smaller scope, not a cut price for the same work.
Work starts only after a signed agreement and a 50 percent deposit. Confirm every payment in your own app, because screenshots can be faked. Never ask clients for passwords, PINs or OTPs.
Workshops
A two-hour positioning workshop
Present the customer evidence
Write differences; dot vote, 3 each
Draft two statements in pairs
Agree what to test, and who does what

A workshop helps a team own the position. Invite the owner and two to five key staff, including riders and sales attendants, who often know customers best. Start with the goal, then the customer evidence.
Everyone writes possible differences, and each person gets three dots to vote. Pairs draft two statements. End by agreeing what to test, and send the actions in writing the same day.
Measuring results
Tolu's laundry, three months later
Claim only results you measured. Label practice projects as practice.
Before: 10 orders from 40 enquiries = 25%
After: 15 from 45 = about 33%
Average order: 3,500 to 4,900 naira
Discount requests: 6 down to 2
Note other changes, like a new estate

Agree measures before launch, so you can compare. Tolu logs enquiries and orders. Before the new position, 10 of 40 enquiries became orders, 25 percent. Three months after, 15 of 45, about 33 percent.
Her average order rose from 3,500 to 4,900 naira, because customers send all their work shirts at once. Discount requests fell from 6 to 2 a month.
She also notes a new estate opened nearby, so she does not credit everything to the brand. That honesty is what makes a case study believable.
Key points
Remember
Ask why until the cause is actionable
Your rate is a floor; explain value
Write scope limits and change requests
Report only measured results

To remember. Discovery finds the real problem. Ask why until you reach a cause you can act on. Your hourly rate is a floor, so explain price with value. Write scope limits and use change requests. And report only results you measured.
